prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case on the shortlist of precision atomic physics that opens genuinely new fundamental tests. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the Doppler and recoil shifts while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once, and Ye's group then pushed the systematic uncertainty and stability to about 1e-18. At that level one sees the gravitational redshift across millimetres, can search for drifts of fundamental constants and can compare clocks across continents. The result has been reproduced and compared in many independent laboratories (RIKEN and Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL), and agreement between clocks is exactly the kind of robust, quantitative test I trust. The attribution is also the cleanest of any candidate: one proposer and first demonstrator, one leader of the record-accuracy and many-body programme, two names that fit the three-person limit with room to spare. The discovery is not driven by technology; it is a new way of looking at what atoms can tell us, even if the applications to geodesy and the second will follow.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the committee has already honoured precision measurement in this corner of AMO physics: frequency combs in 2005 (and Ye was Hall's close collaborator there) and ion control and ion clocks in 2012. A sceptic can call this a further, incremental step in the same metrology line, and the headline application, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened. Priority among the early lattice-clock demonstrations (Katori, Ye, and the Paris and other groups) is not fully clear to me from memory, and the credited pair does not include contributors such as Lemonde or Ludlow. If the committee prefers a prize about a new many-body phenomenon rather than about a measurement instrument, B016 would be the more natural AMO choice.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a measurement advance of the first rank, very mature and arguably overdue, with a clean two-name credit, while noting that the exact priority dates of the magic-wavelength proposal are recalled from memory.
responses.response: I agree with the core and I am glad that a colleague who works on measurement puts it first independently. I would qualify the word 'overdue': maturity here is real but the redefinition of the second is still pending, and I would not make that the reason. The reason is that the clocks give new physics tests (redshift over millimetres, constants), not only better numbers. On the priority dates, I too cannot settle the Sr-lattice history from memory, so the expert report should check it before we write the citation, but I do not think it changes who the two names are.

responses.point: Olsson places aberration-corrected microscopy first as a new tool that opened sub-angstrom imaging of atoms and defects, and ranks the lattice clock only sixth, with a worry that it is an incremental precision step after combs and ion clocks.
responses.response: I take the overlap worry seriously and have listed it as my main reservation. But I disagree that the clock is incremental. Combs gave a way to count optical cycles and ion clocks showed single-particle control; the lattice clock combines a magic-wavelength trap with a very large number of atoms and so changes the stability and the systematic budget by orders of magnitude, and that is what opened the new tests. I also respect the microscopy case, but I see it as an enabling instrument whose physics discovery content is thinner; I would want us to ask whether the physics committee would be rewarding a discovery or an engineering achievement there.

responses.point: Johansson places circuit QED first as the natural continuation of the 2025 prize and as a basic quantum phenomenon made controllable on a chip, and flags his own possible conflict of interest.
responses.response: I appreciate that he states the conflict openly. I think circuit QED is a strong field, but I share Kroll's worry that it follows only one year after the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in the same circuits, and I would keep it as an alternative rather than first. I also note that Girvin's role in the 2004 proposal cannot be credited with the three names we have, which makes the theory side of the citation less clean than the two-name lattice-clock credit. I would be happy to see it rise if the committee wants a second line of AMO-type quantum technology, but not before this.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first for opening neutrino astronomy with a clear, original result, while noting that allocation among Halzen, Spiering, Karle and the AMANDA and Baikal precursors is debatable.
responses.response: I ranked IceCube sixth, mostly because I defer to astroparticle colleagues, and I would like to hear Danielsson on it. As someone who prizes the unexpected, I do find the discovery of a diffuse flux persuasive. My reservation is the one he himself raises: the sources are still only partly identified, and a three-name list from a very large collaboration is delicate. Compared with that, the lattice clock has a simpler attribution, but I accept that this is an argument about tidiness and not about merit, and I do not want to let tidy credit decide the matter.

responses.point: Mehlig puts the quantum spin Hall and topological insulator candidate first as a clean, general mechanism protected by a Z2 invariant, with very wide influence and long independent confirmation, though the neighbouring 2016 prize makes novelty a little delicate.
responses.response: I find the conceptual case strong, and I defer to him and to Eriksson on condensed matter. My concern is practical, namely attribution: Kane and Mele are the theory, but Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal and are not among our credited names, and our members propose three different triples. I would like to see that settled before this goes to the top. If the committee finds a defensible triple, I would regard it as a serious competitor to the clock, and I would put it ahead of the aberration-corrected microscopy.

uncertainties: Whether the committee gives weight to the pending redefinition of the second, or treats the lattice clock as a further step in the combs and ion-clock metrology line.
Relative credit for the earliest lattice-clock demonstrations among several groups, and whether a contributor outside the credited pair would have to be considered.
Whether the topological insulator candidate can be given an agreed triple of laureates, since that would change the ranking of the leading candidates.
statement.conflict_note: No formal recusal is clearly required for the lattice-clock candidate. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund attosecond group and with Ursula Keller's group, which is close to the attosecond theme but not to any shortlisted candidate. As a theorist in atomic, molecular and optical physics I will be careful in judging the AMO entries (B016, B001). No specific personal tie to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile.
